findings.finding: Insights: After 20 rounds each binary score 0‑2²⁰‑1 appears exactly once, so final ranking is a permutation of runners. Pairings must respect equal scores; faster always wins. Count permutations realizable by such “Swiss‑style” pairings. Compute v₂(N), v₅(N) → k = min(v₂,v₅). Beware assuming all 2²⁰! permutations possible; constraints limit N. Use recursive counting of ways to assign faster runners to higher‑score leaves while maintaining equal‑score pairings.

Insights: After i rounds each binary pattern of i wins appears 2^{20‑i} times, so final scores are a permutation of 0…2^{20}‑1. A runner’s score is determined by the round they first meet a faster runner (they lose there). Thus the final ranking equals the order of “first‑loss rounds” for each speed. The tournament constraints force a binary tree where each node pairs two equal‑score groups; the faster of the two groups’ members all beat the slower group’s members. Hence the possible rankings are exactly the linear extensions of the poset where for any two runners a<b (by speed) the first‑loss round of a must be ≤ that of b, with strict inequality when they eventually meet. This poset is a complete binary tree of depth 20, giving N = (2^{20})! / ∏_{v} (size of subtree_v). Compute k = ν_{10}(N) = ν_2(N)+ν_5(N). Use Legendre’s formula on factorial and subtract subtree contributions. Finally output k mod 10^5.

Insights: Final scores are 20‑bit binary win‑patterns; round i groups runners by identical higher‑bit prefixes. Any pairing within each group is allowed, faster wins. Thus achievable orderings = all linear extensions of the poset where runner a precedes b iff a’s speed rank is higher in the first round they differ. This poset is the Boolean lattice of 20 bits ordered by lexicographic (binary) comparison. Number of linear extensions = product over all antichains of factorials of their sizes = ∏_{k=0}^{20} (C(20,k)!) . Hence N = ∏_{k=0}^{20} (C(20,k)!). v₂(N)=∑_{k} v₂(C(20,k)!), v₅ similarly. Compute v₅(N)=∑_{k} (C(20,k)−s₅(C(20,k)))/4, where s₅ is sum of base‑5 digits. Result: v₅(N)=? (≈ 2 × 10⁶). v₂(N) larger, so k=v₅(N). Return k mod 10⁵. (Key pitfall: mis‑interpreting ties – ordering counts permutations within equal scores.)

Insights: Scores form binary numbers; final ranking = permutation of runners to leaves 0…2²⁰‑1. Feasibility ⇔ at each node (size 2^m) the right half can be matched to left half with every left paired to a faster right. For total order this holds iff after sorting the node’s runners, the right set contains the m fastest (i.e., each prefix has ≥ as many right as left). Thus a permutation is valid iff for every k (1…2²⁰‑1) the set of first k ranks contains at most ⌈k/2⌉ right‑side positions. Counting such permutations equals the number of linear extensions of the “binary heap” poset, known to be the product ∏_{i=1}^{2^{20}} C_i where C_i are Catalan‑like binomial ratios. Compute v₂(N), v₅(N); k = min(v₂,v₅). Then output k mod 10⁵. (Key pitfall: ensure equal‑size split condition and Hall’s theorem reduces to prefix condition.)

Insights: Final scores are 20‑bit win‑patterns; each runner gets a unique binary number iff the tournament can realize any bijection between speeds and patterns. The pairing rule forces that after each round scores split groups evenly, so the set of possible final rankings equals the number of linear extensions of the “binary tournament poset” where i beats j iff i is faster and they can meet. This poset is the Boolean lattice B₍₂₀₎ ordered by inclusion of win‑sets. Hence N = number of linear extensions of B₍₂₀₎ = (2²⁰)! / ∏_{k=0}^{20} (C(20,k)!). Compute v₂(N) and v₅(N) via Legendre’s formula; k = min(v₂,v₅). Finally output k mod 10⁵.

Insights: Final scores are distinct binary strings (20 bits). Pairings create a full binary tree; each internal node forces the max label in its right subtree > max in left. Thus a labeling of leaves 1…2²⁰ is valid iff for every node max(right) > max(left). Count such labelings = number of “binary increasing trees” = product_{i=1}^{2²⁰} C(i‑1,⌊(i‑1)/2⌋). Compute N, find largest k with 10^k|N, output k mod 10⁵. Pitfalls: ensure distinct scores, treat max‑condition correctly, handle huge factorials via exponent of 2 and 5 only.

Insights: Final scores are a permutation of all 2^20 binary strings. Any bijection of runners to these strings is realizable because each round’s groups always have equal 0/1 counts, allowing arbitrary pairings. Hence N = (2^20)!. Compute v₁₀(N)=v₂(N)∧v₅(N); v₂((2^20)!)=2^20−1, v₅((2^20)!)=⌊2^20/5⌋+⌊2^20/25⌋+…; k=min(v₂,v₅). Return k mod 10⁵.

Insights: Final scores are distinct binary numbers → ranking = recursive split into equal halves. After each round, winners must form a “ballot” set (prefix winners ≥ losers). Reachable permutations = those built recursively by choosing any ballot half, ordering each half recursively, then concatenating. Compute N = #distinct permutations for n=2^20 via DP on subsets using Catalan‑type counts; then k = min(v₂(N),v₅(N)). Pitfalls: assume ties (none); ensure ballot condition, not any half. Use memoization; avoid double‑counting permutations from different splits.

Insights: Final scores are unique 20‑bit numbers; ranking = permutation of runners onto these numbers. At each node (size 2^r) winners (1‑bits) must be matchable to losers (0‑bits) where each winner is faster than its paired loser. This is a perfect‑matching problem in a total‑order bipartite graph. Compute N = number of leaf‑labelings (permutations) satisfying Hall’s condition at every node. Use recursion: for a set of size 2^r, any split into two equal halves is allowed iff the “winner” half can be matched to the “loser” half (i.e., there exists a perfect matching respecting speed). Count such splits recursively; N = ∏_{r=1}^{20} a_r where a_r = number of admissible partitions of a 2^r‑set. Then v₂(N), v₅(N) give k = min(v₂,v₅). Compute k mod 10⁵. Pitfall: assuming all permutations possible; need Hall’s condition for each node.

Insights: Final scores are 20‑bit strings; each round splits a group of size 2^m into winners/losers of size 2^{m‑1}. Possible winner sets for a 2m‑group = Catalan_m.  
Thus  
\(N=\prod_{j=0}^{19}C_{2^{j}}^{\,2^{19-j}}\) where \(C_n=\binom{2n}{n}/(n+1)\).  

Compute 5‑adic valuation: \(v_5(N)=\sum_{j=0}^{19}2^{19-j}\,v_5(C_{2^{j}})\).  
Use \(v_5(C_n)=v_5\!\big(\binom{2n}{n}\big)-v_5(n+1)\) with Legendre’s formula (carries in base 5).  

Values \(v_5(C_{2^{j}})\) for j=0…19 are  
0,0,0,1,1,0,2,1,0,1,1,3,3,4,0,2,3,5,4,6.  

Summing gives \(v_5(N)=121 818\).  
\(v_2(N)=2^{19}-1=524 287>v_5\), so \(k=v_5(N)=121 818\).  

Answer: \(k\bmod10^5=21 818\).  

Pitfalls: assume ties impossible (they aren’t – each leaf is unique); use correct exponent formula for Catalan numbers.
